title: Stars and Satellites over Gemini North
caption: Satellite streaks beside the Gemini North telescope
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The broken streaks left of Gemini North are satellites crossing the sky, identified by the gaps in their trails. Gemini North is one of the two telescopes of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates with partial support from the U.S. National Science Foundation.

The night sky is always moving, even if the naked eye cannot tell. A long exposure records that motion as trails left by stars, meteors and, more and more, satellites in orbit around Earth. Satellites have long been vital tools in fields such as hydrology and geology, but in recent years their numbers have soared for new uses such as broadband internet access.

Most satellite constellations cannot be seen with the unaided eye, especially where skies are already light-polluted. Sensitive camera detectors on telescopes like Gemini North pick up their reflected light easily, and that light affects astronomical data. NSF NOIRLab is working to reduce the impact of satellites on observations and to protect the sky near observatories from all light pollution.

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph by Jeff Warner. No camera or exposure details or color mapping are published.
understand.eye: Most satellite constellations are invisible to the unaided eye, and the camera's long exposure turns their passage into streaks.

explore: NSF NOIRLab co-hosts CPS, a center for protecting dark and quiet skies, which was recently renewed for a 5-year extension. The photographer, Jeff Warner, documents how the sky is changing as satellite launches increase.
alt: Broken streaks of satellite light crossing the sky to the left of the Gemini North telescope, among star trails.
